threads._README: RESEARCH THREADS — topics that spawned a trail of docs, handoffs and carts. Declared by topic (like `subsystems`): the generator auto-collects every doc/ADR whose filename matches a `match` term, splits them into notes/handoffs/decisions, unions the carts that cite them (via the strong-signal scan), and computes the date span. AUTOMATIC: a new matching doc/handoff/cart folds in on the next `node tools/build-history.js` with no editing. The only hand-authored part is `title` + the voiced `blurb` (follows guides/voice.md); leave `blurb` empty and a structural sentence is derived instead.

items.title: Roads & a world to drive on
items.blurb: This one started small and would not stop. The idea was just to vary procplaces' roads-and-cities generator — split density into land-use and intensity, kill the grid look. Then it hit the wall: arced roads. You can't bend a road on a global grid without everything downstream quietly lying about where it goes. So roadnet threw the grid out for a node-lattice of splines — local, deterministic, infinite, honest. That cracked it open, and then it just kept going: a street level under the map (the fill language in lotfill, then cityplan's whole procedural town), real junctions (interchange), the at-grade streets (streetlab, all the way to a typed OpenDRIVE cross-section), the traffic that actually lives on them (trackgen — lane-keeping, crossings, right-of-way, even police chases). And sloop — the cart that actually drives the thing — is the whole reason it had to be true and not faked. The latest turn went philosophical: ADR 0021 says the road geometry lives in plain 2D, the pseudo-3D view is just an adapter, and the field-based road renderer proves it. Many handoffs deep, still open. The longest thread in the project, and the one most likely to eat another month.

items.title: The instrument-engine ports
items.blurb: Almost every voice in here is a port of navkit, done one at a time until the whole modeled orchestra existed — pluck, reed, the jet-flute pipe, guitar and piano straight off StifKarp, the bowed string, and brass last. The rule we learned the hard way: port the oscillator verbatim, don't "improve" it on the way in — every shortcut showed up later as a tuning scar (the waveguides go flat at the top of the keyboard; still chasing that one). Four handoffs and a dedicated tuner cart are the receipts. Trust your ears over the label — the doc says Rhodes, the ear says no, the ear wins.

items.title: The effects bus
items.blurb: The engine quietly turned into a mixing console. It started as 'effects are recipes, not primitives' — don't ship a reverb knob, ship the settings that make a space — and then the bus grew teeth: drive, echo, tape, the auto-wah that got built wrong once and torn out and redone right. The big call was making effects per-instrument and reorderable instead of one master strip, so a chorus can sit on the Rhodes alone and the order of the chain is yours. The boutique-pedals roadmap is the wishlist that keeps feeding it.

items.title: The radio stations
items.blurb: The stations are the part that plays itself. Each one is a genre studied blind first — write the ideal band from the music, before reading how the last cart did it, so the library doesn't homogenize — then built: a seeded song, a chord brain, voices picked to match. The blind-briefs are that first honest sketch; the genre-fidelity ledger is the brutal follow-up that says where we faked an instrument or skipped a brain. Bossa, dub, house, satie, a dozen more. The dream underneath is tinyjam racks — radios as song generators you can actually edit.

items.title: Mobile & touch
items.blurb: A desktop toy meeting a phone, and the phone winning a lot of the arguments. Real device testing turned up the stuff you can't reason about from a chair — the five-touch iPhone ceiling, phantom touches, fingers that swipe-tap-do-five-things-and-crash-it. Out of that came the loupe (a magnifier so you can actually grab a tiny knob), the shared widget kit so every cart handles mouse, touch and keyboard at once, and a couple of audits that swept every cart for whether a phone could even play it. Not glamorous. Load-bearing. Late on, the thread flips the question from 'can a phone play it' to 'can every cart reshape itself to any screen' — a framebuffer that grows on demand, iOS carts filling the glass with safe-area insets and rotation, and the densest instrument racks rebuilt to reflow, until a device matrix and a responsive-instrument-ui playbook write the moves down.

items.title: Spatial audio
items.blurb: Sound in space, done in two passes in basically a day. First the OpenAL move: a listener, voices with positions, automatic pan and distance-volume and Doppler in flat 2D pixel space. Then the better idea — move a whole effected source as one object, so its reverb tail and shimmer travel with it instead of staying nailed to the center. Small thread, but it's the one that makes a passing car sound like a passing car.

items.title: Making work into a game
items.blurb: Somewhere in here a second project woke up inside the first one. Not a game and not an instrument — a sim about work itself: what a worker costs, when it's worth hiring one, what your own two hands are worth against a machine that never gets tired. thecut and handwork are the first probes, the sloop-production notes are the thinking out loud. It's the second north star written down plainly — deep honest sims under a lo-fi surface — and it's the part most likely to quietly become the main thing.

items.title: Making it fast without breaking it
items.blurb: Late in the window the question stopped being 'what can it do' and started being 'how cheap is it.' A fleet-wide CPU survey, a stress cart that does nothing but hammer the fill rasterizer, and a first real optimization — solid spans collapsed into a single rectangle instead of a pixel at a time — with the old path kept right beside it so you can prove the new one matches. Then the big swing: batching draw calls didn't pan out (a captured null result), so instead of fighting the GPU, skip it — rasterize the whole frame on the CPU into one framebuffer and blit it once. The software-canvas probe ran the experiment for real and came back GO: byte-identical to the GPU path, cityplan from 11.4ms to 5.0ms a frame. Honest about the limit, though — it's a win for pset-bound carts, not everything. And going to the CPU forced a harder question the GPU hid: is rotation even deterministic across machines? The det-probes chased that to the floor — gap-free rotated fills, cross-arch libm trig quantized, RotSprite benchmarked head-to-head. The rule the guide writes down: optimize in a loop you can't fool — measure, change one thing, measure again, keep the A/B.

items.title: Playing together
items.blurb: For a long time every cart was solo. This is the thread that let a second person into the same one. It started as the smallest honest version — lockstep over UDP on a LAN, every machine running the identical simulation off the identical inputs, nobody's server deciding the truth — and climbed a rung at a time until it left the house: a blind relay that forwards bytes without ever understanding the game (so one relay serves every cart), rooms you join by a code, a play-together button on the site, and finally a relay-free peer-to-peer path over WebRTC, Mac to iPhone in about twelve milliseconds. The discipline underneath is lockstep's oldest rule — send the inputs, not the state, and trust every copy to land in the same place. The moment they don't, everything's wrong at once, which is why it's gated by an echo-mirror twin that catches the drift before a human could.

items.title: Getting it out, and getting it found
items.blurb: Making a good thing turned out to be only half of it. This thread is the other half: a way out to people who don't already know it exists. First the door — carts bundled into one app, signed and notarized, uploaded to TestFlight. Then the harder half, getting found: a keyword lab that measures what a listing can actually rank for, screenshots composited (not stretched) to exact device sizes, a self-contained press page, promoted purchases that surface in search, and a marketeer that maps a cart to its tribe and the venues where that tribe already gathers. The rule the notes keep insisting on: the tools prepare the vocabulary and the numbers, but a human writes the prose — no auto-generated press kits, because a stranger can smell a robot. It's the newest thread, and the one that admits good work doesn't sell itself.

items.title: The workshop tools itself
items.blurb: The other half of the work is the work on the workshop. Not carts — the tools that make carts, read them, and keep them honest. It runs on two fronts. One is the editor as an environment in its own right: carts that are themselves tools in a shared space (cart-os), a design system for the IDE chrome, wireframes built as carts, an information architecture for where a cart's media actually lands. The other is the project learning to read itself: every cart owning its own metadata so the index becomes a generated view, frontmatter written for the next agent as much as the next human, driftable numbers that flag when a doc's arithmetic goes stale, a checks-and-oracles map that answers 'I changed X, what do I run,' and the spec() safety net that pins gameplay logic the way the audio gates pin sound. The honest admission underneath it all — teaching-gaps, tools-we-need — is a project keeping a running list of what it still can't do.

items.title: Teaching it chords
items.blurb: For a long time the carts could make any SOUND and had no idea what a chord was. A station played a progression because someone typed the progression in. This thread is the part that learned the theory — and it went both directions, which is the whole point. First generate: a roman-numeral vocabulary with per-style Markov tables, so a station can pick its own next chord in the idiom. Then ANALYZE: hand it a progression and get the numerals back, in key, with an honest question mark when it doesn't know. That second half is what a player actually needs, because it's the half that can answer 'what could come next' about a song you wrote rather than one it wrote. The extraction followed the usual law — harmony.h only came out of bossa and cocktail once a second cart wanted the same tables, and the tables had already drifted a bug-fix apart by then. Then it stopped being a brain and became an instrument: eleven modes, a dozen genre style tables, a band that plays them, and bandbox, where the chord chart IS the sequencer and the per-cell locks are the idioms mined back out of the radio carts' own bar moves.

items.title: Bodies that fall over properly
items.blurb: Two layers, and the cheap one came first on purpose. A tiny shared verlet toolkit did the ropes, cloth, blobs and ragdolls for weeks, with each cart owning its own arrays and step loop — deliberately not a rigid-body engine. Then Box2D got vendored for the things verlet can't do honestly, and the shelf that grew on top of it is the interesting part: a sprite region becomes a small polygon and gets textured from its own verts, so the paint covers the hull exactly instead of approximately. What the puppets then taught is subtractive. Placing every bone where the maths says it goes, every frame, gives you a shape being carried through a move — nothing contacts anything, nothing lags, nothing overshoots, and it reads like card. Drive ONE body and let the other fourteen hang off it through their joints and it reads like a body, because late and imperfect is what a skeleton does.

items.title: Running the same cart everywhere
items.blurb: Write it once in C, run it as a native window, a web page and a phone app — that promise only holds if the seam between the cart and the machine is drawn in exactly one place. This is the thread that draws it: a platform layer thin enough that the same source hits clang, emcc and Xcode without the cart ever knowing, and the renderer decision that makes it possible — a software canvas that rasterizes the whole frame on the CPU, so 'the screen' is just a buffer any platform can blit. From there it's targets: the iOS build ladder and its profiling, wasm audio that has to sound bit-for-bit like the native mix, and a feasibility look at the Switch. The rule is the boring one that makes portability real — one seam, and no per-platform forks in cart-land.

decisionNotes._README: Voiced one-liners for the 'Roads not taken' cards (and any decision worth a readable line), following guides/voice.md — replaces the dry ADR context paragraph on the page. Keyed by ADR basename without .md. No entry = fall back to the ADR's first-paragraph summary.
decisionNotes.0001-cut-coroutine-process-model: The DIV process model — the thing we'd put on the box as what PICO-8 doesn't have — got cut in week one. A coroutine per game object sounds great until you're writing the C-side scheduler instead of the game. Killed it before it could set the shape of everything after it.
decisionNotes.0008-cut-turtle-graphics-api: Shipped a whole Logo turtle, nine functions, then went looking for who used it. One cart. Out it came — a feature with one user isn't a feature, it's a maintenance bill.
decisionNotes.0013-cut-music-api: music() was the PICO-8 half of the sound plan: pattern banks, four channels, the works. Nobody ever called it — we'd already picked code-first music twice over. This is the exact fork where sound stopped being a tracker and started becoming a synth.
decisionNotes.0014-cut-unused-convenience-helpers: Three convenience helpers, zero carts using them, each the less-loved sibling of one that caught on. The usage audit found them; we cut them. Convenience nobody reaches for is just more surface to keep working.
decisionNotes.0033-youtube-first-video-distribution: The carts had been making little videos for a while with nowhere to put them. This picks YouTube first and says why: it's the one channel with a real API you can push to unattended, so the last mile can be a tool instead of a chore. TikTok got looked at and stays a manual web upload, because its API only accepts drafts.

observations._README: Cross-week RETROSPECTS — conclusions that only surface from reading the whole arc back at once, NOT legible commit-by-commit. Distinct from each era's `editorial` seam (which annotates one era from inside it); these look down on the entire window. Each `evidence` line is grounded in a number the generator can re-derive from git/index.json, so a future refresh can re-check it. Refresh by re-running the `recipe` against the current window and rewriting `items` + bumping `asOf`.
observations.title: Retrospect — reading the whole arc back
observations.recipe: How these were got, kept so it can be done again in due time: after the history page + spine are written, read them BACK as a finished whole — the rendered docs/history.html (which now mines design-doc CONTENT automatically: the per-era 'design-note spotlight' pulls each doc's friendly one-liner from docs/README.md + the carts that cite it, and 'Roads not taken' surfaces the cut ADRs), this spine, and the raw counts (`git log --since=<from> --date=short --pretty=%ad | sort | uniq -c` for per-day density; `grep -o '"subsystem": "[a-z0-9]*"' history-spine.json | sort | uniq -c` for the milestone mix; cart/ADR totals). Then ask the question that started it: "since we've written the docs/history code and text, can you now read it back and come to insights/conclusions you couldn't before?" Mine the negative space too — STATUS.md's 'Decided-against' ledger + the cut-* ADRs + the handoff docs (where work got parked) are as telling as what shipped. This refresh also reads the two present-tense sources the page now renders as the FRONTIER band (a capstone beside the retrospect — the retrospect looks back, the frontier shows the open edge NOW): docs/HANDOFF.md's active lanes (via `node tools/handoff.js --json`) and the polish debt from `node tools/cart-todos.js --count` (surfaced as a NUMBER, never the list). A landed lane simply drops off — so the frontier is deliberately NOT woven into any dated past era. And re-check the RESEARCH THREADS (threads.items): a new window can start a long investigation no thread yet catches, or spawn docs an existing thread's match misses — declare a new thread or widen a match so it folds in (threads auto-collect by filename, but the topic + voiced blurb are hand-authored). Past refreshes added the 'multiplayer'/'storefront' (then 'workshop'/'portability') threads and extended 'mobile' to adopt the device-adaptive docs; the 07-10 pass widened engines (unison, portapop), storefront (export-ratios, 320x200), optimization (engine-simplification), workshop (flight-recorder, editor-cart-workflow) and mobile (acidrack-layout). Rule: every claim cites a derived number, so it stays honest with the repo like the rest of the page. The 07-30 pass (weeks 9-10) added the two threads a whole window had outgrown — `harmony` (the chord brain, seeded bossa-rack.md) and `physics` (Box2D + the verlet layer, seeded box2d-integration.md) — and widened five existing match lists to adopt the new docs (engines→synth-secrets/rubberband/morphdrum, storefront→video-distribution/app-icon-mask, mobile→responsive-first-device-face/canvas-density-spectrum, radio→bandbox, workshop→lab-experiments). Three things this pass learned about the METHOD, worth keeping: (1) its new items cite git/index.json numbers instead of milestone counts. That was written as a workaround for the 07-10 milestone gap, and the SAME DAY's backfill closed the gap — but keep the habit anyway, because the backfill then invalidated eight older evidence lines that did quote milestone counts, which is the cost of denominators that move. A git-derived number does not move; and (2) re-reading old items is part of the pass, not optional. Observation 4 was carrying a figure that was true when written and wrong by the time of the refresh (07-10 cited at 118, finished at 172), and its central claim needed a recorded counter-example rather than a quiet edit. Expect one such correction per refresh; a retrospect that only ever grows is not being re-read. The 07-30 backfill produced the sharpest example so far: observation 13 said audio had stopped being the majority, which was true of the data then and wrong within three weeks — audio came back to 54% of weeks 9-10 once the Synth Secrets audit started. That correction was only VISIBLE because the milestones were backfilled onto the same basis, which is the argument for closing a coverage gap rather than annotating it: an under-measured window does not read as an error, it reads as a trend. Caveat learned: per-day commit counts shift with timezone/day-boundary choices — cross-check before calling any single day a peak or a lull (the apparent '06-13 lull' was a date-grouping artifact). PROMOTION PASS (the loop-closer, added 2026-07-10 — a meta-audit found observations consistently terminate at prose while only ONE gotcha had ever become a lint): for each NEW observation, and any new CLAUDE.md gotcha born this window, ask two questions — is the lesson mechanically checkable, and does a gate for it exist? Checkable-and-ungated → promote it NOW: a check in the matching lint (lint-carts' source hazards, lint-docs, repo-doctor's roster) or at minimum a task→gate row in docs/guides/checks-and-oracles.md. An observation that stays prose must earn it by being judgment, not mechanics. Precedents: set-and-hold effects → lint-fx-frame.js; watch()-format-string + built-in shadowing → lint-carts.js (both 2026-07-10).

items.title: It became a synthesizer with a screen
items.body: The stated identity is a learn-C fantasy console in the PICO-8 lineage. The revealed identity, in aggregate, is a software studio that happens to render graphics: 14 modeled instrument engines, a reorderable effects bus, MIDI, and positional audio. Each synth commit reads as 'just another cart' alone — only the pile shows sound ate the project. And this isn't only emergent: VISION.md and design/second-north-star.md name the shift outright ('a second pursuit has grown up alongside it… it now drives much of the work' — deep honest sims behind a lo-fi surface), so the git aggregate is confirming a turn the project already saw in itself.
items.evidence: 161 of 384 milestones are audio (78 sound + 32 machines + 26 radio + 24 effects + 1 modrack ≈ 42%) — a clear majority through week 3 (38 of 60 ≈ 63%), then NOT the largest thread from week 4 through week 8 as roads, iOS and the store/promote threads grow, then the majority again in weeks 9–10 (see observation 13, which this refresh had to partly reverse). 'sound' is the largest of 26 subsystems by a wide margin; mobile is 2nd at 33 and roads 4th at 32. NOTE: these full-window figures come from the 07-30 backfill, which extended milestones through 2026-07-30; they read 67 of 208 when written, covering only through 07-10; the pivot is documented in design/second-north-star.md (REFLECTION, 2026-06-09).

items.title: The fantasy console kept amputating its own fantasy-console features
items.body: The page celebrates what shipped, but the negative space is just as revealing: the project repeatedly removed PICO-8/DIV-style conveniences to keep the from-scratch lesson honest and code-first. The DIV coroutine/process model — billed in VISION as the headline differentiator from PICO-8 — was cut in WEEK ONE. Turtle graphics shipped, then was removed for one user. The music() pattern-bank was cut because the project had chosen code-first music twice over — which is the same decision that sent audio down the synthesis road (observation 1). Three zero-adoption helpers went after an API-usage audit. The throughline: subtract anything that lets the learner skip the real thing.
items.evidence: Four cut-ADRs: 0001 (coroutine model, cut 2026-05-30, week 1), 0008 (turtle graphics removed 2026-06-01), 0013 (music() → code-first, 2026-06-04), 0014 (3 unused helpers, 2026-06-04); plus STATUS.md's 'Decided-against / deferred' ledger.

items.title: One spec set three weeks' trajectory
items.body: The navkit instrument-port spec, written on 06-02 in the 'subsystems born' era, is the keystone. Trace it forward: the spec → the engine-port marathon (PLUCK→BRASS) → which created the demand for effects (all those voices need processing) → which created the mixing console (they need routing) → which created spatial audio (they need placing). Most of the last two weeks is downstream of one week-1 planning artifact, not one feature.
items.evidence: Spine flags it 'seeds the entire June sound saga'; the engine milestones it spawned span 06-05 (PLUCK) through 06-10 (BRASS, 'the last engine').

items.title: Throughput compounded — it never plateaued
items.body: The week-1 tooling (harness, profiler, libtcc live backend, make-cart + parallel Workflow batches, the radio.h/ui.h/keybed.h chassis) was the real product: weeks 2–3 are almost pure content riding that scaffolding. The marked-day note calls 06-05 'the densest day yet' — true when written, but it's since been beaten many times over, and the all-time peak keeps moving: 06-22 held it at ~150 for a week, then 06-30 broke it at 160 — and the window keeps clearing 100 to the end (07-01/02/03 all over 116, then a lighter mid-week-6 tail before a 101-commit finale on 07-07 — and week 7 repeats the shape in miniature: two catch-up days in the 60s, then the all-time peak on 07-10). Those late peaks rode the original scaffolding AND each new layer built on top of it (the self-knowledge tooling of observation 9, then the multi-cart app pipeline). The investment never stopped paying off as accelerating output. TWO CORRECTIONS from the 07-30 refresh, both the kind this observation keeps earning. First, 07-10 was cited here as 118 when this was written mid-day; it finished at 172 and is now the all-time peak by a clear margin, so the ranking below has been redone. Second, and more interesting: the compounding claim finally meets a counter-example. Weeks 9-10 hold a genuine lull (12, 2, then 7 commits on 07-24, 07-25 and 07-27) after nine weeks that routinely cleared 100. It is not a plateau in capability, since 07-30 immediately puts up 73 and the densest research of the whole project sits inside those same two weeks, but 'it never plateaued' can no longer be said of the raw daily count. Output stopped being the thing that was compounding; the window's biggest days are audit and correction days, not shipping days.
items.evidence: Per-day commits (git log --since=2026-05-28 --date=short --pretty=%ad | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn): week 1 runs 18–60; weeks 2–3 routinely break 100. Top five now 07-10=172, 06-30=160, 06-22=150, 06-10=138, 07-03=136, with 06-04=129 and 07-02=128 behind them; 06-05=106. The 07-19→07-30 window runs 36, 98, 45, 88, 69, 12, 2, 21, 7, 38, 30, 73 = 519 commits over 12 days. Author-date and committer-date agree on 07-10=172, so the peak is not a day-boundary artifact (the caveat in the recipe). 546 carts total, up from 511 at the start of the window.

items.title: Every shared header is crystallized duplication — always in that order
items.body: The library headers under runtime/ never lead; they trail. radio.h was extracted after a dozen stations; keybed.h after seven keyboard carts; ui.h after hand-rolled widgets; pointer.h was retrofitted across the remaining hand-rolled-pool carts. ADR-0006 makes this deliberate — the engine doesn't own these, they precipitate out of cart-land once the pain is felt. Abstraction trails repetition every time.
items.evidence: radio.h 'extracted as the shared station chassis' (06-05); pointer.h 'adopt across the 13 remaining hand-rolled-pool carts' (06-13); keybed.h 'seven carts migrate onto' (console-midi era).

items.title: The audio system recapitulated the history of studio gear
items.body: It isn't one 'sound' blob — it's four strict layers, each presupposing the last: synthesis (instruments exist) → effects (instruments get processed) → console (instruments get mixed/routed/reordered) → spatial (instruments get placed in space). You can't have a mixing-console day until 14 engines and bus effects exist to mix; you can't place a signal until there's one worth placing. The order was emergent, and it matches how real studios evolved.
items.evidence: Era sequence: engine-marathon (synthesis) → fx-truecolor (effects) → console-midi (console) → spatial (placement), 06-08 through 06-15.

items.title: Long unresolved threads are only visible in aggregate
items.body: A single commit hides the threads that run across weeks. The auto-wah is described as 'the scar finally resolved as a bus effect' — implying an earlier parked attempt that sat unbuilt while a cheaper per-voice stand-in held the place. The engine marathon is the same shape: a goal declared early ('until every modeled timbre exists') and closed out only at BRASS. The whole-arc view is what surfaces these.
items.evidence: audio-notes.md still names a 'PARKED §8.10 bus wah' beside the per-voice cousin; auto-wah milestone resolves it in the fx-truecolor era (06-11).

items.title: A second project woke up inside the first
items.body: For three weeks the revealed identity was 'a synthesizer with a screen' (observation 1). The tail of the window adds a second current that isn't sound at all: production and economy sims — thecut, handwork — where the subject is labour, cost and delegation, not graphics or audio. It reads as the second-north-star reflection (06-09) finally cashed out into carts rather than prose: deep honest sims under a lo-fi surface. Too young to call a third pillar at week 3's end, but it's the first work in the window that's neither a game, an instrument, nor a tool — a new category, and the one the project then seemed most curious about. Week 4 acts on that curiosity (beltworks, a factory economy) and starts wiring it into a bigger whole — see observation 10.
items.evidence: Production/economy-sim carts: thecut + handwork (06-17, citing design/sloop-production.md + design/second-north-star.md, REFLECTION 2026-06-09), then beltworks (06-22, a Factorio-lite factory builder) — the window's only carts whose subject is economy/labour rather than graphics or sound.

items.title: The project built a mirror to read its own corpus
items.body: Three weeks of accumulation produced ~400 carts; week 4 is when the project turned around and built the machinery to UNDERSTAND that pile. Almost all in one day: cart-index.js (a computed 'what teaches what' index), the spec() cart-logic harness (deterministic regression tests for game logic — the gameplay twin of week 3's audio gates), the ★ techniques compendium in the editor, the teaches/lineage convention promoted to a required, controlled-vocabulary index.json field, cart-dupes.js (cross-cart duplication → refactor candidates), and teaching-gaps.md (what the API offers but no tutorial teaches). This is a new KIND of work — not engine, not content, not even the guard-rails of week 3 (which verify correctness); it makes the corpus legible to itself. And it obeys the same law as observation 5: you only build a technique index once there are ~400 techniques to index. The mirror trails the corpus, exactly as abstraction trails repetition.
items.evidence: A new 'introspect' subsystem debuts at 5 milestones in a single day (2026-06-22), and 06-30's self-knowledge day (observation 15) grows it to 9, week 7's field-note 019 to 10 — tied for 4th-largest of 25 subsystems when written, and 17 of 26 (8th) after the 07-30 backfill added the ledger and handoff audits; cart-index.js / spec.js / cart-dupes.js / the compendium / the teaches[] hard-gate all born 06-22; 456 carts in index.json.

items.title: The carts began assembling into one game
items.body: Through week 3 the carts were standalone — an instrument, a toy, a sim, each complete in itself. Week 4 is the first time they're treated as PARTS of a larger whole. A showreel/teaser design note is written 'for the larger game', a big-game backlog enumerates per-cart remaining work plus the cross-cutting seams, and a clip+reel pipeline is built specifically to show the assembled thing (clips now carry audio; compose-clips stitches them into a reel with transitions). Underneath, the pieces converge: streetlab draws the streets, beltworks the factory economy, facegen the people (procedural street portraits + a conversation system), with interiors and street-level content briefs behind them. This is observation 8's 'second project' growing past sims-as-experiments into a game-in-assembly — roads + economy + NPCs + interiors named as one backlog, not four.
items.evidence: Born 2026-06-22: design/showreel-teaser.md ('for the larger game'), the big-game backlog (per-cart work + cross-cutting seams), interiors-brief Round 2, the streetlevel-content stub; the clip pipeline (make-gif clips-carry-audio + compose-clips reels) the same day; facegen's conversation system; a v0 reel cut from 5 carts (sloop/interiors/dialogue/thecut/moog).

items.title: The scrutiny turned from the corpus to the canvas
items.body: Observation 9 was the project building a mirror to read its own CORPUS. The last two days of the window turn the exact same scrutiny one level down — onto the rendering itself. The question stops being 'what can it draw' and becomes 'is what it draws honest, and is it cheap.' The software-canvas probe answers the cheap half by skipping the GPU entirely: rasterize the whole frame on the CPU and prove the result byte-identical to the old path (cityplan 11.4ms→5.0ms). The det-probes answer the honest half: rotated fills, strokes and sprites are gap-free and — once libm trig is quantized — identical across architectures, which is the property the GPU was quietly NOT giving. And the same correctness machinery shows up as graphics gates: road-check and mirror-diff are framebuffer oracles that assert pixel invariants headless, the visual twins of week 3's audio gates and observation 9's spec() harness. It's the third domain to grow a guard rail — audio, then game logic, now pixels — always after the thing it guards already exists, never before.
items.evidence: 2026-06-24: software-canvas Phase 0 GO (cityplan 11.4ms→5.0ms, byte-identical, ADR-flagged GO); det-probes rotfill/rotline/rotspr/textrot with cross-arch libm-trig quantization; road-check.js born 06-24 + mirror-diff.js born 06-23 (both golden-framebuffer oracles); the 'perf' + 'gfx' subsystems each pick up new milestones the same day.

items.title: The roads thread finally grew a city to drive through
items.body: Observation 7 named the roads work as the project's longest unresolved thread — 'started small and would not stop.' June 23–24 is where it stops being just roads. Three city sims wake up on top of the street layer in two days: gridcity simulates the city as feedback (land value ↔ crime ↔ pollution ↔ power ↔ water ↔ fire ↔ RCI demand), cityplan plans it (procedural lots and building interiors as one town), trackgen makes it live (traffic with right-of-way, crossings, K-turns, police chases), and cityview lets you look at it in pseudo-3D. This is the convergence observation 10 predicted — the strands assembling into one artifact — but it's also load-bearing for observation 8's 'second project': a city you can simulate, plan, drive and view is exactly the world the production/economy sims need to sit inside. The honest footnote: overpass was born, lived a few hours as a standalone flyover sandbox, and got folded into cityview the same day — the corpus grows by merging as much as by adding.
items.evidence: Born 06-23: gridcity (SimCity data-layer sim), cityplan (lots + interiors merge). Born 06-24: cityview (four-mode pseudo-3D), linecompare; overpass born-and-deleted (folded into cityview). trackgen traffic-AI Phases A–C (cross-roads, right-of-way reservations, chases) across 06-23/06-24; field-based road rendering + road-check + ADR 0021 (geometry in 2D, view is an adapter) on 06-24.

items.title: Audio stopped being the majority
items.body: For three weeks the revealed identity was 'a synthesizer with a screen' (observation 1) — audio was the majority of everything the project shipped. The back half of the window is where that ends, and not because audio slowed: the instrument racks of 07-02 are some of the richest sound work in the whole repo. It ends because everything ELSE accelerated at once — a real city to drive, the engine running on a phone, a way out to the store. The synthesizer got a screen, then the screen grew a city, a device and a storefront around it, and the sound became one thread among several instead of the trunk. REVERSED IN PART by the 07-30 backfill, and it is the most interesting thing that pass turned up. Once weeks 9–10 were measured on the same basis, audio was the majority AGAIN — 54% of that window's milestones — because the Synth Secrets audit put the whole synth engine back under the microscope and produced twenty days of almost nothing but sound work. So the honest shape is not a decline but a dip: audio was the trunk, then one thread among several for five weeks, then the trunk again the moment someone asked whether the trunk was actually correct. Both halves stay, because 'the share keeps sliding' was a true reading of the data available then and a wrong guess about what came next.
items.evidence: Audio's milestone share falls from 63% through week 3 (38 of 60) to 32% across weeks 1–7 (67 of 208, the figure available when this was written) — then the 07-30 backfill puts it at 42% across weeks 1–10 (161 of 384) and 54% within 07-11→07-30 alone (94 of 175), the highest concentration since week 3; by the last several eras the largest threads are 'store', 'roads', 'ios' and 'mobile', not sound. Yet the instrument work itself never stopped — acidrack, tracker, yachtrack, pocketbox, delia and otafamily are all born on a single day, 07-02.

items.title: The project grew a way OUT — a distribution layer
items.body: Every prior week made THINGS — engines, carts, sims, tools, guard-rails. The last week is the first that builds a way to RELEASE them. de_switch_cart gives each cart its own audio/video/sprite-sheet context so many run in one binary; build-app.js turns a manifest into a multi-cart app; the same manifest builds a signed+notarized Mac .app and runs on iOS with in-app purchases; and a whole ASO/store/press pipeline (research → compose → score → screenshots → press page) sits around the build. This is a new KIND of work again — not engine, not content, not tool, not the guard-rails or the mirror of observations 9/12 — it's distribution. And it obeys the same law as every layer before it: it trails the thing it distributes. You only build an app pipeline once there are hundreds of carts worth shipping.
items.evidence: The distribution cluster debuts across weeks 5–6 — as of 07-07: ios (10 milestones), store (7), netcode (5) and the new promote (4), 26 together, 06-29→07-07; after the 07-30 backfill those four read 13 / 15 / 6 / 10 = 44, store the fastest-growing of them because the pipeline stopped being built and started being used (observation 31); ADR-0023 (ship carts as apps, not the editor; 06-29), ADR-0026 (store pipeline in-house, not Fastlane; 07-03), ADR-0027 (sound state via the request queue; 07-03); the umbrella app gets its name, 'Tiny Jam' (07-03).

items.title: The mirror got a second day — and became a habit
items.body: Observation 9 caught the project building a mirror to read its own corpus — almost all in one day, 06-22. Six days later it did it again, bigger, and this time the one-off scripts became permanent EDITOR surfaces. build-context gathers a single cart's scattered docs; its horizontal twin topic-brief does the same for a whole feature; lint-xrefs finds the missing backlinks. Then the views: the ★ design board and the ★ reflections page, both reading a shared doc-status.js that owns the lifecycle vocabulary. And the closing move was pure honesty — an audit of all 15 field notes recording what each actually became, flipping the journal from 10 observed / 0 incorporated to 10 incorporated. The introspection layer stopped being a burst and became infrastructure the editor carries.
items.evidence: 'introspect' grows from 5 milestones (06-22) to 9 — adding build-context, topic-brief + lint-xrefs (432 missing backlinks → 42), the board + reflections pages, and the field-notes audit, all 06-30 — then 10 with week 7's field-note 019 (4th-largest of 25 at the time; 17 and 8th of 26 after the 07-30 backfill, which added status-check, the HANDOFF cleanup and the LAB pattern); the ★ design board + ★ reflections ship as editor Docs-tab views the same day.

items.title: A guard-rail decision got reversed by making the thing cheap
items.body: ADR-0024 (06-29) settled the on-device renderer: the software canvas is canonical for 2D, and 3D stays off the initial iOS list — because textured triangles measured ~10fps on the phone. That reads like a permanent limit. It lasted six days. On 07-02 a single optimization — sw_tritex's scan-box clamp and hoisted plot — made textured triangles hundreds of times cheaper, and on re-measurement 3D held ~59fps on the same class of device, overturning the ADR's exception. The lesson isn't 'the decision was wrong'; it's that a guard-rail written against a measured cost is only as fixed as the cost. The rail wasn't relaxed — the thing it fenced off got fast enough to let back in.
items.evidence: ADR-0024 puts 3D off the iOS list after ~10fps tritex (06-29); sw_tritex clamp + hoist lands 07-02 (infiniminer 1204→3.4ms, 358×; podracer 89→6ms) and the on-device re-measurement (infiniminer 10.9ms @59fps on an A13) overturns the exception the same day.

items.title: The corpus learned to reshape itself to the glass
items.body: For most of the window each week ADDED to the corpus — a new engine, a new sim, a new instrument. Week 6's dominant thread does the opposite: it makes what's already built fit any device. The framebuffer moves to the heap and grows on demand (byte-identical, so nothing renders differently), iOS carts fill the screen with safe-area insets and rotation, and a run of the densest UIs in the repo — acidrack, acidwire, epianofit, scalegrid — are rebuilt to reflow, the practice then frozen into a responsive-instrument-ui playbook and ADR-0028's sensible-defaults rule. It's the same law as the mirror (obs 9/16) and the guard-rails (obs 12/17): a general capability (device-adaptive layout) only precipitates once there's a big corpus to apply it across, and it trails that corpus. A whole week spent not adding but ADAPTING.
items.evidence: The 'mobile' subsystem reaches 10 milestones by 07-10 (growable framebuffer, the ui-audit responsive-layout gate, acidwire, responsive-instrument-ui, then hint(), disclose.h and finger_px()) — and 33 after the 07-30 backfill, 2nd-largest of 26 and the biggest non-audio thread in the repo, because weeks 8–10 spent the control vocabulary, the eight acidwide arrangements, face.h and the whole iPad rack on exactly this problem; the change ships NO new engine primitive — the growable framebuffer is byte-identical to the fixed one; device-adaptive-layout is the largest active handoff lane (6 docs — see the frontier band).

items.title: Shipping wasn't enough — it built the demand side too
items.body: Observation 14 caught the project growing a way OUT — distribution, getting a cart to the store. Week 6 builds the OTHER half of the funnel: getting it found once there. The trailer builder turns a manifest into a demand-generating video; asc-push marks promoted purchases so IAPs surface on the product page and in search; the leads marketeer maps each cart to its tribe and the venues where that tribe gathers; and the editor's information architecture resolves the whole workflow into Make / Promote / Ship — promotion elevated to a first-class verb with its own per-cart tab, bracketed by Ship, with Dream as the zeroth verb closing the loop to a cycle. The project stopped assuming good work sells itself.
items.evidence: A new 'promote' subsystem debuts at 4 milestones — the trailer builder (07-04), the leads marketeer (07-07), promoted IAPs via asc-push --promote + Store.swift PurchaseIntent (07-07), and Make/Promote/Ship (07-07) — and grows to 7 as the tab itself ships end-to-end plus the one-take-many-ratios export pipeline (07-08); leads tunes music-tribe coverage to ~90%; the editor gains a per-cart Promote tab (design/promote-tab.md).

items.title: The longest thread started generating its own cities
items.body: Observations 7 and 13 tracked roads as the thread that 'would not stop' and then 'grew a city to drive through' — but those roads were hand-placed or pulled from OpenStreetMap. Week 6 turns the corner from DRAWING roads to GROWING them: a rung ladder climbs four steps in a single day, generating a realistic street network from a population-density field and per-city tensor-field arterials, extracted into a shared world spine (worldnet.h) the moment a second cart consumed it (obs 5's crystallized-duplication law again). And it's fenced by a NUMBER: sndi-check scores a generated network against real cities on a street-network-disparity composite. That makes it the fourth domain to grow a deterministic oracle — after audio, game logic, and pixels (obs 12) — now network realism; and true to obs 12's rule, the oracle (rung 0) shipped before the generator it judges.
items.evidence: worldgen rungs 0–3 all land 2026-07-06 — sndi-check (rung 0), worldnet.h (rung 1), citygrow's density field + tensor arterials (rungs 2–3); 'roads' is the 2nd-largest subsystem at 32 milestones (still 32 after the 07-30 backfill, but 4th now — sound, mobile and machines all passed it, and roads gained nothing at all in weeks 9–10); sndi-check is the 4th deterministic oracle after the audio gates, spec(), and road-check/mirror-diff; first generated-vs-real numbers measured (citygrow mean degree 2.65 vs Amersfoort's 2.71).

items.title: A LAN prototype became shipped web multiplayer in one week
items.body: Multiplayer is another thread only legible in aggregate (obs 7's shape). It began as lockstep over UDP confined to a LAN (07-02); week 6 carried it all the way to the open web in two topologies within days of each other — a deployed relay with cart-scoped rooms and a site play-together button (rung 5a), then a relay-free WebRTC peer-to-peer path at ~12ms (rung 5b), built, play-tested and published. A LAN-only prototype became a shipped, hosted, two-topology feature in a single week — the closing, not the opening, of a multi-week investigation.
items.evidence: netcode grows to 5 milestones; rung 5a relay deployed + wss-verified 07-06, rung 5b WebRTC P2P built + published 07-07; the WebRTC spike measured Mac↔iPhone at ~12ms over wifi (07-06).

items.title: The oracle judged the city into existence — four days from metric to drivable streets
items.body: Observation 19 caught the worldgen ladder shipping its oracle (sndi-check) before the generator it judges. Week 7 shows why that order wins: with the number in place, every rung could land, be scored, and stop being an argument. Rungs 4 and 5 fill 310 districts with density-picked street morphs and calibrate the fill against a real city — five SNDi metrics land dead-on Rotterdam and --compare turns the loop into a PASS/FAIL exit code that actually discriminates (the calibrated city passes, arterials-only fails). Then the grammar is extracted to citygen.h and sloop's M key drives it, buildings and all. Four days from 'we can measure a street network' to 'press M and drive a city that never existed' — and the residual gaps (deg-4+ share, circuity) are DOCUMENTED as a structural ceiling of the arterial tensor field, not hidden. The oracle didn't just gate the work; it let the work say precisely where it stops being right.
items.evidence: sndi-check (rung 0) born 07-06; rungs 4–7 + citygen.h + sloop's M-mode + ~6,356 buildings all land 07-10; whole-city T-junction share climbs 1.1%→64.6% (Amersfoort 63%, Rotterdam 60%); the --compare gate: calibrated citygrow fails 0/8 metrics vs Rotterdam, arterials-only fails 5/8; 'roads' milestones grow 24→32 in four days.

items.title: The guard-rails became refactoring licenses
items.body: Every oracle in the repo was built to catch a regression. Week 7 reveals their second job: licensing SUBTRACTION. The engine-simplification backlog opens on 07-09 and within ~36 hours dozens of dedup passes land across the two hottest shared files in the repo — clamp helpers and the SVF/ladder filter cores unified in sound.h, a font table and shared bodies in studio.c, a 121-arm dispatch chain flattened to a switch — every one marked behaviour-preserving and proven so by the gates built weeks earlier (tune-check, level-check, the byte-identical render checks). The same licence powers the day's extractions: roadkit.h leaves streetlab byte-identical, citygen.h leaves citygrow's export byte-identical. You can only delete this fast when a machine can prove nothing changed — the oracles turned cleanup from a courage problem into a checklist.
items.evidence: 24 commits since 07-09 whose subjects claim a behaviour-preserving / behavior-identical / byte-identical gate; design/engine-simplification.md born 07-09; sound_fire_req's 121-arm else-if → switch (07-10); roadkit extraction gated by streetlab spec 104/0 + mirror-diff 68=68, citygen by a whole-city export byte-identical to pre-extraction.

items.title: The bake stopped being a one-way door
items.body: For six weeks the .cart.png was an export: source flowed in at bake time and never came back, and sprites had two sources of truth that didn't know about each other — hand-paint a generator cart's sprites in the editor and the next CLI bake silently reverted them. Week 7 closes the loop in both directions inside 48 hours: de:meta.slug anchors every baked cart to its source file and gets backfilled across the fleet, a save-to-source button writes Code-tab edits back to tools/carts/<slug>.c (Gap 1), and sprite-patch ships the pixel round-trip as a slot-level overlay (Gap 2, Option D) — with a flight recorder capturing every editor run as a keepable take on the side. The editor stopped being a viewer of baked artifacts and became a full peer of the CLI: an edit made anywhere now has a path home.
items.evidence: The editor-cart-workflow gap ledger closes three entries in one window — Gap 1b slug (07-08) + fleet-wide backfill and lint-required (07-10), Gap 1 save-to-source (07-10), Gap 2 sprite-patch round-trip (07-10); the flight recorder (always-on capture + keep-to-clips) lands the same day; 456 carts carry the slug anchor.

items.title: Three headers crystallized in one day — the law became a reflex
items.body: Observation 5 named the law: shared headers never lead, they trail — radio.h after a dozen stations, keybed.h after seven keyboards. Week 7 runs the law three times in a single day: citygen.h precipitates out of citygrow the moment sloop needs to drive the generated city, roadkit.h out of streetlab the moment citydrive needs its curb returns (with roadlab's interchange grammar following by evening), and disclose.h out of acidwire's hand-rolled disclosure model three days after that model was first written. The cycle time collapsed — radio.h took a week of stations to crystallize; disclose.h took 72 hours from first hand-rolled copy to shared header with its consumer migrated. The project no longer waits for the pain to accumulate; it recognizes the shape on the second consumer and extracts on the spot, gates and all.
items.evidence: runtime/citygen.h, runtime/roadkit.h and runtime/disclose.h all born 2026-07-10 (git --diff-filter=A), each landing WITH a consumer already migrated (sloop / streetlab+citydrive / acidwire) and a byte-identical or behavior-identical gate; acidwire's disclosure model hand-rolled 07-07, graduated 07-10; ADR-0006 is the standing rule they precipitate under.

items.title: It hired an outside auditor, and the auditor was a magazine column
items.body: Every guard rail up to now was internal and asked the same question: does it still do what it did? The audio gates, spec(), the framebuffer oracles, canvas-diff — all of them compare the engine to a previous version of itself. Week 9 does something the project had never done: it measures the engine against an outside claim about what it SHOULD do. Gordon Reid's Synth Secrets, 63 monthly parts across five years, read as a sieve over runtime/sound.h one instrument family at a time. That is a different kind of test and it found a different kind of defect — not regressions, but places where a voice had been built on a guess nobody had ever checked. And the framing was right from the first line: nothing here is a bug report, several divergences are deliberate, they get recorded anyway so the choice stays a choice instead of decaying into an accident.
items.evidence: docs/design/synth-secrets-audit.md born 2026-07-28, the sieve marked COMPLETE the same day across eight recipe passes (§E brass, §F strings, §H plucked, §I pianos, §J drums, §K flutes, §L Hammond, §M effects) plus the §A–§D architecture pass; ~106 sub-findings, turned into synth-secrets-plan.md's ordered ledger; 519 commits 07-19→07-30 with the audit and its build plan the largest single thread.

items.title: The most valuable thing the audit produced was the refusals
items.body: A canonical text is easy to treat as an authority, and this one explicitly is not. Reid contradicts himself between Part 10 and Part 47 and retracts the earlier claim, which the audit had quoted as law and had to correct in its own text. Of the seven Phase 1 items, two are recorded DROPs: the brass envelope loses all three of its numbers on measurement, and the Hammond item was simply mis-priced. Phase 2's biggest item had its PREMISE fail — the piano's dispersion chain turned out to be inert and its stretched tuning was being cancelled a frame after note-on, so the thing being tuned wasn't reaching the sound at all. Then 2.3(b) was dropped because the finding count that ranked it was a false premise: four of its five families have no inharmonicity to modulate in the first place. The rule that made this productive is in the plan doc: nothing is skipped, an item not worth doing gets a recorded DROP with its reasoning. Negative results are the output, not the waste.
items.evidence: synth-secrets-plan.md records 1.4 brass + 1.6 Hammond as DROPs and 2.3(b) DROPPED on the owner's call; §C12 corrected by the §F strings pass (Reid's own retraction); 2.3's premise failed on measurement (dispersion inert + stretch cancelled post-note-on), both fixed and shipped as MODE_PIANO_STIFF; 17 commits 07-19→07-30 whose subjects carry drop/revert/refused/premise-failed language, including two reverted PSOLA phase fixes and a Rubber Band objection 'tested and refused'.

items.title: Being wrong in the test rig, and writing that down too
items.body: The honesty rule gets its hardest test here and holds. On the dispersion work the owner's ear killed an A/B that the numbers had blessed — and was right, because the comparison was confounded by decay rather than timbre. The resolution commit says the quiet part out loud: dispersion costs no sustain, step 2 works, and both of the earlier failures were the agent's own, in the test rig, not in the engine. That is a different claim from 'the feature was hard.' It means two rounds of measurement had been measuring the harness. The same shape repeats on the PSOLA popping hunt, where two phase-lock attempts each regressed a different face of the feature and both got reverted, and the fix was not a third guess but an oracle — psola-check, with three detectors because each is blind to a defect the others catch, which then killed a third attempt in one command. The pattern across both: when a measurement and an ear disagree, suspect the rig.
items.evidence: 07-30 commit run: 'the owner's ear killed the A/B and was right — it was confounded by DECAY, not timbre' → 'I4b RESOLVED: dispersion costs no sustain, step 2 works — both failures were mine, in the test rig'; 07-26: both PSOLA phase fixes reverted, then psola-check.js born and documented as killing a third failed epoch attempt in one command that had previously cost several listen-and-report rounds.

items.title: A whole class of bug came into view: the control that was never wired
items.body: This is the genuinely new failure mode of the window, and it only became visible because the project stopped adding and started auditing. In twelve days it found: every ui.h widget in a five-version rack dead the entire time, two finished piano sliders unreachable because instrument_mode rejected two of its own indices, an aux-parameter channel whose width had to agree in five places so a mismatch made a parameter silently do nothing, a pan knob whose useful range was buried past 4 Hz, an effect that picked from eight LFO shapes and never said which, a muted guitar string treated as fret 0 so every power chord had a third in it, and a golden render gate that had been red for twenty days because nobody ran it. None of these crash. None fail a test. Each one looks exactly like a working feature. The response was two rules and two linters rather than seven fixes: 'a gesture nobody can see is not a control' went into the control vocabulary, lint-aux-params was written for the silently-inert parameter, and the software-canvas golden got wired into repo-doctor so it cannot rot unnoticed again.
items.evidence: 07-28 'hyperbox v6: every ui.h widget in the rack was dead, v1 through v5'; 07-29 'instrument_mode rejected idx 2/3, so two finished piano params were unreachable' → tools/lint-aux-params.js; 07-29 control-vocabulary rule 6; 07-30 pedalboard's autopan SPD range, the unnamed LFO shape, the fret-0 mute, and 'canvas-diff: re-bless drawall's golden — red for 20 days, nobody ran it' + the repo-doctor wiring.

items.title: Seven new oracles, and they exist to settle arguments rather than catch regressions
items.body: Observation 12 called the guard rails the third domain to grow one, always after the thing it guards. This window builds seven more in twelve days, but their purpose has shifted. tune-check and level-check were built to notice a change; ab-render, click-check, stereo-check, inharm-spec, disp-model, psola-check and lint-aux-params were built to end a disagreement — is this partial where a stiff string would put it, did that morph splice, is the flag even reaching the DSP. Two of them are worth naming for what they revealed about the previous set. stereo-check exists because every other audio gate averages left and right at the door, which means the pan law, the stereo soft clip, chorus width and autopan had exactly zero coverage — and a mono downmix is actively blind to antiphase panning. And disp-model is analytic rather than empirical, written specifically so a coefficient search doesn't have to hold a shared engine broken while parallel agents compile. Oracles stopped being a safety net and became an instrument.
items.evidence: Born 07-19→07-30: ab-render.js, click-check.js, stereo-check.js, inharm-spec.js, disp-model.js, psola-check.js, lint-aux-params.js (git --diff-filter=A over tools/); synth-secrets-plan.md credits four of them to 'nothing existing could see the bug'; ab-render exits nonzero when two variants render byte-identical audio, i.e. when the flag never reached the DSP — a bug that had already cost one bogus finding.

items.title: The mirror finally turned on the bookkeeping
items.body: Observations 9 and 16 tracked the project building machinery to read its own corpus, then making that machinery permanent. The blind spot was the records themselves. STATUS.md was the doc every other doc said to trust and the only one held to no standard — both linters carve it out, and neither can see a ledger losing sync with the repo, because none of that is a broken link. Same for HANDOFF.md, the place you go to resume complex work. On one day both got audited: status-check.js was written for the ledger and immediately found that 20 of 53 'open' items had already shipped, plus an entry being used as a headline that was hiding three more. HANDOFF went from 1356 lines to 649 and 19 lanes to 9 — and the sequence is the part worth keeping, because the seven facts that existed nowhere else were MOVED OUT before anything was deleted. handoff.js's own --check turned out to be guarding three holes it looked like it covered. Nine weeks of trusting the map, then one day of checking it against the ground.
items.evidence: tools/status-check.js born 2026-07-30; commit 'STATUS: 20 of 53 open items were already shipped' and 'the headline was being used as an entry, and it hid three shipped things'; HANDOFF.md 1356 → 955 → 751 → 649 lines across a numbered six-part cleanup with 'MOVE the 7 facts that existed nowhere else, BEFORE deleting anything' as step 2 and ~18 factual corrections in step 3; handoff.js --check audit found three holes; ledger now reads shipped 46 · open 42 · cut 13.

items.title: Distribution stopped being a pipeline and became two apps in review
items.body: Observation 14 caught the project growing a way OUT and noted it trailed the thing it distributes. This is that pipeline being used in anger, which is a different milestone from building it. acidcandy became Tiny Acid Jam — named, priced at $1.99 one-time, iconed, screenshotted, described in the maker's own voice, versioned 1.0 and pushed to App Store Connect. Then pedalboard grew GUITAR IN and became Tiny Pedal Board, a second app, on the same rails. What is telling is where the friction turned up: not in the build, but in the last mile of store bureaucracy, so asc-push grew --category, --age-rating, --price, --content-rights and --review-contact one submission blocker at a time, and the verified first-submission runbook got written down with an explicit split between what the tool automates and what still needs the web UI. The icon got its own oracle too, measured out of Apple's own renderer rather than guessed — because a hand-drawn rounded rect has circular corners where the real mask has continuous ones, and that had already shaved two apps.
items.evidence: 07-19 Tiny Acid Jam renamed/priced/iconed and logged shipped to ASC; 07-22 apps/pedalboard scaffolded → named Tiny Pedal Board → screenshots + listing + description + version 1.0; asc-push gains --category/--age-rating/--price/--content-rights/--review-contact across 07-22; docs/design/app-icon-mask.md + tools/icon-mask.js born 07-28 with the mask MEASURED from Xcode's ictool and matched to device ground truth at mean 0.13px; HANDOFF lane L45 reads 'an APP IN REVIEW'.

items.title: Mockups became the design method, and the grammar trailed the mockups
items.body: The responsive work had been a retrofit for weeks: take a cramped UI, make it reflow. This window inverts it, and the way it inverts it is the interesting part. acidwide draws EIGHT complete arrangements of one unhidden 303 in a single day, draw-only, nothing wired — a control rail, a full knob row, a step strip, a tappable pitch grid, the unpaged version, the alignment-preserving version, the paged version. roomyface does four more for a tablet. Only after all of that does the practice get written down as a layered plan, and only then does face.h ship as a grammar that declares zones and enforces the rules, proved on three carts the same day. Then the winners went into production and the loser was deleted: the iPad ROOMY layout climbed mockup to shipped in about forty commits and the old 2×2 rack was removed rather than kept as an option. Observation 5's law again, in a new material — the grammar could only be written once eight arrangements existed to generalize from.
items.evidence: acidwide arrangements A–H all committed 2026-07-20 as draw-only mockups; docs/design/responsive-first-device-face.md's L0–L4 plan written the same day, then runtime/face.h + tools/carts/deviceface.c born with proving passes on chipjam, dubjam and grooveface; roomyface B/C/D + acidcandy_ipad mockups 07-22; 'acidcandy: remove the old 2x2 rack, promote ROOMY to THE tablet view' 07-23.

items.title: Harmony went bidirectional, and that is what made it an instrument
items.body: For nine weeks the carts could synthesize anything and knew nothing about music. A station played a progression because a human typed the progression in. The harmony work fixes that, and the shape of the fix is the finding: generating chords is the easy half and the half that doesn't need you. A brain that only generates gives you a machine playing to itself. The moment it could also ANALYZE — hand it a progression, get the numerals back in key, with an honest question mark when it doesn't know — it could answer a question about a song the PLAYER wrote, which is what a chord assistant is for. Everything downstream needed that direction: chordwise suggesting a next chord with a reason, the improv soloist snapping strong notes to the current chord's tones, and bandbox, where the chord chart IS the sequencer. Extraction obeyed the usual law and confirmed it in the most literal way available: harmony.h only came out once a second cart wanted the same tables, and by then the two copies had drifted a bug fix apart.
items.evidence: harmony-brain.md brief → runtime/harmony.h extracted from bossa + cocktail (byte-exact) 2026-07-20, chordwise born the same day as the analyzer side; grows to 11 modes + genre style tables 07-21; improv.h chord-aware soloist + four adopting carts 07-20/21; bandbox born 07-21 and wired to spec 131 green by 07-22; the drift is recorded verbatim on 07-22 — 'the tables have now drifted a fix apart twice' — as the argument for a band.h extraction.

items.title: The puppets taught the lesson by subtraction
items.body: Box2D arrived with a shelf and six carts in a day, which is the normal shape by now. What is worth recording is what one cart learned over the following week, because it inverts the instinct. boxhuman's first working handstand PLACED all fifteen bones every frame with their velocities zeroed, which is the maximally authoritative approach and produced something that reads as a shape being lifted, turned over and put back — nothing contacted anything, nothing lagged, nothing overshot. The fix was to give up almost all of that authority: drive ONE body, the pelvis, and let the other fourteen hang off it through their own joints. Three stronger approaches were tried and each failed in an instructive way — writing the transform loses the trajectory to the children's mass, making the root kinematic fires the whole figure into the air because an infinite anchor absorbs every reaction, and torque alone is too weak to be carried through a 180-degree turn. A motor against the ground with finite force was the answer, and the cart's own comment names why it works: nothing is teleported and no velocity is fabricated, so momentum and contact stay real.
items.evidence: runtime/boxrig.h + six Box2D carts born 2026-07-23; boxhuman 07-29 → 07-30 goes one figure → five builds off one rig table → per-build attitudes → the staged handstand → 'the pelvis rides the turnover, the other fourteen bones hang off it' (383 insertions), with all three rejected approaches and their measured failure modes recorded in the source; docs/design/box2d-puppets-and-playground.md.
